title: A rural route, a PO box, and a named lot all have an address with no street number at all
assumption: Every valid street address begins with a number.

input.description: An address-line validator that requires the first token to be numeric, used on a shipping or billing form.

what_goes_wrong: Entirely legitimate, deliverable addresses are rejected because they don't start with digits — rural routes, PO boxes, and named-lot rural properties are all real addressing conventions with no house number.
why: A leading street number is just one of several addressing schemes in common use; postal systems also deliver to rural route numbers, post office boxes, and named lots or stations that never had a house number assigned at all. A regex that hard-requires a leading digit encodes 'suburban street address' as if it were the only valid addressing format, when it is only one of several.
affects: any address validator requiring a leading street number

repros.code:
import re
pattern = re.compile(r"^\d+\s")
for addr in ["Rural Route 2", "PO Box 445", "Lot 7 Orchard Lane"]:
    print(addr, bool(pattern.match(addr)))
repros.expected_output:
Rural Route 2 False
PO Box 445 False
Lot 7 Orchard Lane False

Rural Route 2 false
PO Box 445 false
Lot 7 Orchard Lane false

fix: Don't require an address to start with a number; if you need structured address fields, make the house-number field optional and let 'address line 1' accept free text, which is how postal services themselves treat it.

sources.title: Michael Tandy: Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Addresses

test_cases.note: A PO Box is a deliverable address with no street number; your form should accept it.
